questions.question: How does Banker’s Algorithm determine if a resource request is safe?

answers.b: It checks if granting the request keeps the system in a safe state
answers.c: It grants resources only to the highest-priority process
answers.d: It denies all requests unless all resources are free

explanations.a: Randomly granting resources can lead to unsafe states and potential deadlocks.
explanations.b: The algorithm simulates granting the request and verifies if the system remains in a safe state before actual allocation.
explanations.c: Banker’s Algorithm does not prioritize requests based on process priority; it checks system safety instead.
explanations.d: Denying all requests until all resources are free is inefficient and not how Banker’s Algorithm functions.

questions.question: What must be true for a system to be in a safe state?

answers.a: All processes have received their maximum resources
answers.b: There exists at least one sequence in which all processes can complete
answers.c: No process is waiting for resources
answers.d: The system has no running processes

explanations.a: A system can be in a safe state even if not all processes have received their maximum resources.
explanations.b: A safe state means at least one sequence exists where all processes can complete without deadlock.
explanations.c: A process can still be waiting for resources in a safe state as long as deadlock is avoidable.
explanations.d: The system can be running processes while maintaining a safe state.

questions.question: If a system is in an unsafe state, what does that imply?

answers.a: A deadlock is certain to occur

explanations.a: An unsafe state does not guarantee deadlock but increases its risk.
explanations.b: Recovery depends on future resource allocations and system behavior.
explanations.c: An unsafe state means there is no guaranteed way to avoid deadlock, but it is not certain to occur.
explanations.d: An unsafe state does not require a system shutdown.

questions.question: Which data structure is essential for Banker’s Algorithm?

explanations.a: Stacks are used for function calls and recursion, not resource allocation tracking.
explanations.b: Queues are used in scheduling, but Banker’s Algorithm primarily relies on matrices.
explanations.c: Banker’s Algorithm relies on matrices to store resource allocation, availability, and process needs.
explanations.d: Linked lists are not used for storing resource allocation data in Banker’s Algorithm.

questions.question: Which situation can lead to starvation in Banker’s Algorithm?

answers.a: A process constantly requesting more resources than available
answers.b: The system having an infinite number of resources
answers.c: The system being in a safe state
answers.d: All processes running at the same time

explanations.a: A process that constantly requests more resources than available may never get executed, leading to starvation.
explanations.b: If the system had infinite resources, starvation would not occur.
explanations.c: A safe state does not guarantee resource allocation fairness; starvation depends on request patterns.
explanations.d: All processes running simultaneously does not necessarily cause starvation.

questions.question: How can Banker’s Algorithm be modified to handle multiple resource types?

answers.a: By maintaining separate allocation and need matrices for each resource type
answers.b: By allowing only one type of resource
answers.d: By preventing new processes from starting

explanations.a: The algorithm maintains separate matrices for each resource type, allowing it to handle multiple types efficiently.
explanations.b: Restricting to one resource type makes the algorithm less practical for real-world scenarios.
explanations.c: Increasing system memory does not directly impact Banker’s Algorithm.
explanations.d: Preventing new processes from starting is not an appropriate modification.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of Banker’s Algorithm?

explanations.a: O(1) implies constant time complexity, which is not the case for Banker’s Algorithm.
explanations.b: Banker’s Algorithm has a worst-case complexity of O(N²M), where N is the number of processes and M is the number of resource types.
explanations.c: O(N!) is an impractically large complexity and does not apply to Banker’s Algorithm.
explanations.d: O(log N) is more common in tree-based algorithms but not in Banker’s Algorithm.

questions.question: Which scheduling strategy complements Banker’s Algorithm?

explanations.a: FCFS does not consider resource allocation constraints, making it less compatible.
explanations.b: SJN focuses on minimizing execution time, not resource allocation safety.
explanations.c: Priority Scheduling complements Banker’s Algorithm by ensuring higher-priority processes receive resources first while avoiding deadlock.
explanations.d: Round Robin focuses on time-sharing, which does not align with Banker’s Algorithm.

questions.question: If a process requests resources but the system remains in a safe state, what happens?

explanations.a: If the request does not lead to an unsafe state, the system grants the resources to the process.
explanations.b: The request is only denied if granting it results in an unsafe state.
explanations.c: A process is not terminated simply for requesting resources.
explanations.d: Deadlock occurs only when there is a circular wait and no available resources.
